name: Ethiopia
card_headline: Federal forces took Mekelle in October after war resumed in Tigray, while Fano and the OLA fight on and Eritrea has cut ties.
card_summary: War resumed in Tigray on 23 September, and federal and allied forces entered Mekelle in early October, installing a six-month caretaker administration. The TPLF and six other armed groups, including Fano and the OLA, say they have allied to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who began a new term on 5 October after a June election that Tigray did not vote in. Eritrea cut ties on 1 October, and clashes continue near Rama and Badme. Drone strikes have killed civilians in Amhara and Tigray.
card_local: Addis Standard reports a drone strike on 29 October that residents say killed 16 people at an Amhara displacement camp, and Borkena tracked the Tigray airport seizures and the ICRC evacuation from Mekelle. State-run ENA carries the government line on the Tigray administration. [1][2][3][4]
card_international: AP and AFP report the collapse of the 2022 Pretoria deal, a six-month caretaker government in Tigray and drone strikes that killed at least 25 civilians on 29 and 30 October. [5][6][7]
card_scholar: Critical Threats tracks fighting at Rama and Badme and an unconfirmed Eritrean build-up at Sawa, while Chatham House and Crisis Group describe a zero-sum fight that could pull in Eritrea and Sudan. [8][9][10]
context_md: The Pretoria agreement of November 2022 ended the 2020 to 2022 war between the federal government and the TPLF. [11] Ghent University researchers estimate that war caused about 500,000 civilian deaths, and the deal left territory, security and accountability disputes open. [5] The national electoral board cancelled the TPLF's registration in May 2025, which barred the party from the June 2026 vote. [12] In Amhara, fighting between government forces and the Fano militia ran through 2025, with both sides committing serious abuses according to Human Rights Watch. [13] The government has also fought the Oromo Liberation Army in Oromia since 2018. [14] Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea became independent in 1993, and Abiy now says sea access is a national need. [15] The UN estimated 3.3 million people were internally displaced by mid-2025. [13]

sections.title: Tigray: Pretoria is dead, Mekelle is held by Addis Ababa and the front has moved to Rama
sections.body_md:
The collapse came in stages. In April the federal government extended the mandate of Tigray's interim chief administrator, Tadesse Werede, for a year. [4] Between late April and 5 May the TPLF pushed him out and installed a council led by its chair, Debretsion Gebremichael, according to Crisis Group. [10] On 23 September Tigrayan forces seized Mekelle's airport and detained federal police posted there, and Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights. [2] The TPLF joined six other armed groups, including the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army, in an alliance that says it aims to remove Abiy. A Crisis Group analyst, Magnus Taylor, called it an "opportunistic military alliance". [5]

Federal and allied Tigray Peace Force fighters then took Mekelle. The TPLF said it had moved out tactically and would keep fighting from other positions. [11] On 16 October the government set up a six-month caretaker administration meant to restore services, return displaced people and prepare an election. [6] Getachew Reda's Simret party and Tigray Peace Force members lead it, and Critical Threats reports disputes among them over appointments and the arrest of at least seven former TPLF officials. [16] On 22 October the commander of the Tigray army, Fisseha Kidanu, said Tigray was still at war. [17]

Fighting has centred on Rama since 7 November, with unverified claims from both sides, and the military has imposed curfews in Mekelle and other towns. [16][8] Casualty data is thin. ACLED counted 253 political-violence deaths in Tigray from 1 January to 21 October, with 115 in September alone, and Frontlines.et put the federal army in control of 53 woredas to the TDF's 19 on 28 October. [18] Hospital sources told the BBC at least 52 civilians died around Alamata in three days, which Africanews relays and nobody has checked. [19]

lenses.local: Borkena reported the airport seizure, the ICRC evacuation of 161 people from Mekelle on 28 September and later drone strikes, but I did not read Tigray Online or Tigray Broadcast Media directly. [2][3]
lenses.international: AP reports the alliance, the caretaker administration and the TPLF's 14 October statement calling Tigrayans who work with the federal government traitors. [5][6]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House says the government has been more cautious than in 2020 to 2022 and calls the TPLF a rogue administration in its messaging, while the Rift Valley Institute had warned in March that the conflict was paused, not resolved. [9][12]

sections.title: Eritrea and the sea: ties cut on 1 October, a border front at Badme and Rama, and no verified troop count
sections.body_md:
Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, and Eritrea then severed relations. [11] Ethiopia's foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, wrote to the UN Security Council on 8 October accusing Eritrea of an armed attack. Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, denies that Eritrean troops are in Ethiopia. [8] The army chief, Birhanu Jula, said on 13 November that Eritrea leads the rebel offensive and shelters TPLF leaders, and he also accused Egypt of supplying the rebels. [8]

Critical Threats records Eritrean and TDF forces fighting the federal army around Badme from 9 November, with artillery and federal drones. ACLED reported Eritrea had regained Badme by 15 November, while other trackers said it had not held it on 12 and 13 November. A report of mass Eritrean mobilisation at Sawa on 14 November is unconfirmed, though satellite imagery showed more activity there. [8] Africa Confidential, cited by the UK Home Office, reported Eritrean units near Idaga Hamus. [18]

The sea is the stated issue. On 5 October Abiy told parliament Ethiopia must secure a Red Sea outlet and promised to work for it on a "give and take" basis. Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia met at New Alamein a day earlier and said only coastal states should govern the Red Sea. [15] On 2 November Egypt and Sudan rejected unilateral Ethiopian management of Nile dams. [16]

A widely shared claim holds that a February letter from Addis Ababa demanded Eritrea leave Assab. AFP Fact Check rated it misleading: the letter asked Eritrea to withdraw troops from Tigray and proposed talks on sea access. [20]

lenses.local: Local sourcing is thin on this front: the Reporter's June editorial says federal agencies allege Eritrean backing for TPLF hardliners and presents it as an allegation, not a finding. [21]
lenses.international: AP says fighting could draw Eritrea into another war next to Sudan, and Al Jazeera's wire copy records Sudan's army chief visiting Asmara twice since July. [5][22]
lenses.scholar: Crisis Group's Alan Boswell names the TPLF's alliance with Eritrea as a key factor in the renewed challenge to Addis Ababa. [23]

sections.title: Amhara: a Fano command claim, a federal drone war and civilians in displacement camps
sections.body_md:
The Amhara Fano National Movement was formally set up in January 2026. Its chairman, Zemene Kassie, told Le Temps that Fano factions from Shewa, Wollo and Gondar operate under one command and that Fano controls more than 80 percent of rural Amhara. He also alleged that federal drones are Turkish-made and bought by the UAE. These are his claims, reported by Addis Standard, and nobody has verified them. [24]

The federal army reports gains. Critical Threats records reported recaptures of Wuchale, Girana, Lipso and Wurgessa between 3 and 10 November, which would secure the A2 highway between Dessie and Woldia. On 16 November the AFNM and the army fought on the B31 highway southeast of Bahir Dar, and the AFNM claimed Debre Werq, which Critical Threats could not confirm. [16][8]

The civilian toll comes mostly through drones. Addis Standard reported that a strike on the Hayiq Jari 2 camp on 29 October killed 16 and injured 22, all figures from residents, with no official count. [1] AFP counted at least 25 civilians killed in strikes that day on that camp and on Rama in Tigray, and the army did not respond. [7] Human Rights Watch recorded a February 2025 strike in East Gojjam that killed 16, and said Fano also abducted and killed teachers. [13]

The army said on 24 September that it had killed 272 TPLF fighters in North Wollo, a figure no one has checked. [22]

lenses.local: Addis Standard is the main local source on the Hayiq strike, and Ethiopia Insight carries a viewpoint arguing that attacks on Amhara civilians in Oromia may amount to crimes against humanity. [1][25]
lenses.international: AFP reports the 29 October strikes and notes that the government stands accused of indiscriminate attacks. [7]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch finds both the army and Fano committed war crimes in 2025 and says aid access in Amhara was severely restricted. [13]

sections.title: Oromia: a church says 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in Arsi, and the OLA joins the alliance
sections.body_md:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said on 26 October that at least 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in two attacks in Arsi Zone: 14 in Merti district on 20 October and 46 in Shirka district days later. The church counted more than 20 seriously wounded and 20 homes burned. The Oromia regional government blamed the OLA, and its spokesperson, Hailu Adugna, said the group wanted to provoke ethnic and religious conflict, with no evidence offered. The OLA could not be reached, and its leader, Kumsa Diriba, has denied that his fighters target civilians. [14]

Critical Threats reports suspected OLA fighters killed Biniam Adugna, a Prosperity Party official, at his home in Fital, North Shewa, on 9 November, citing Wazema Radio. [16] Its 13 to 17 November brief has nothing on Oromia. [8] The OLA is one of the seven groups in the Alliance for Survival. [5]

The 2025 record is similar. Human Rights Watch said fighting between the federal army and the OLA, and clashes among armed groups, caused civilian casualties, and that violence on the Oromia and Benishangul-Gumuz border displaced over 11,000 people in late May 2025. [13] AP notes that internet restrictions limit reporting from Oromia, so most figures here come from one side or the other. [14]

Ethiopia Insight's viewpoint author, Kenaw Tesfaye Akililu, says Amhara civilians have been killed in Oromia since 2022 and that no prosecutions have followed. That is one author's assessment. [25]

lenses.local: Ethiopia Insight's Kenaw Tesfaye Akililu, a human rights researcher on western Oromia, argues that self-defence claims risk hiding possible mass atrocity against Amhara communities. [25]
lenses.international: AP carries the church's toll and the regional government's attribution, and says UN investigators and Amnesty International have documented abuses by both sides. [14]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch documents civilian harm and displacement from the federal-OLA fighting in 2025. [13]

sections.title: A June election without Tigray: 438 of 501 seats, 94 percent turnout and an opposition kept out
sections.body_md:
Ethiopia voted on 1 June. [26] AP reports the Prosperity Party won 438 of 501 seats in the House of Representatives, with turnout of 94 percent among more than 50 million registered voters. Most opposition parties were prevented from taking part, and prominent critics were jailed, exiled or missing. Tigray had no vote and has had no federal representation for six years, and 143 polling stations in Oromia and Amhara did not open because of insecurity. African Union and IGAD observers were mostly confined to Addis Ababa. [27]

The national electoral board had declared results in about 825 of 1,138 targeted constituencies by 6 June, according to the state news agency. [28] The opposition professor Merara Gudina refused to run and called the vote a sham. [27] Abiy was sworn in for a new five-year term on 5 October. [15]

Before the vote, Ethiopia Insight's Eyob Tilahun Abera argued that an election during war could not confer legitimacy, and described campaigning in Bahir Dar as unsafe and travel as restricted. [29] The electoral board had cancelled the TPLF's registration in May 2025, which Rift Valley Institute compares with the 2020 election dispute that preceded the war. [12] The interim Tigray administration is now meant to prepare a regional election within six months. [6]

lenses.local: Ethiopia Insight's pre-election viewpoint is the clearest local critique; the state news agency reports only the counting progress. [29][28]
lenses.international: AP calls the vote marred by insecurity and records the opposition's complaints of harassment. [27]
lenses.scholar: The Rift Valley Institute treats the TPLF's exclusion from electoral politics as one of the unresolved drivers of renewed war. [12]

sections.title: Press freedom: editors detained, licences suspended and a media law that moves revocation power to a prime-ministerial appointee
sections.body_md:
CPJ reports that Bewket Abebe of The Reporter was detained in Humera on 21 March and held three days before release without explanation. Addis Standard's managing editor, Million Beyene, was taken from the newsroom in April by men who said he was needed for questioning, and was held at an unknown location for nearly two weeks. Authorities suspended licences for Deutsche Welle correspondents and Addis Standard, revoked Reuters accreditation and barred an AFP reporter from a flight to Tigray, citing national security. [26]

Human Rights Watch's 2026 report covers 2025. It says at least six journalists and media workers were arrested in August and September, that The Reporter's senior editor, Yonas Amare, was abducted in August and missing for eight days, and that police raided Addis Standard in April. An April 2025 amendment to the media law moved licence-revocation power to a head appointed by the prime minister. [13]

The practical result is thin primary reporting from the war zones. AP could not verify the claims on either side about Mekelle, and Critical Threats leans on social media trackers and Wazema Radio for much of the front line. [11][16]

lenses.local: CPJ quotes Ethiopian journalists who describe intimidation as normal and editors who say they are working in the dark. [26]
lenses.international: Reuters lost accreditation and an AFP reporter was kept off a Tigray flight, according to CPJ. [26]
lenses.scholar: Human Rights Watch ties the arrests to a wider shrinking of civic space, including five suspended rights groups. [13]

sections.title: Humanitarian need: 761,000 displaced in Tigray, a 74 percent funding gap and rations cut
sections.body_md:
The UK Home Office puts Tigray's internally displaced population at about 761,284 at the end of July 2026, up from about 710,000 in June 2025. MSF-supported hospitals admitted more than 700 war-wounded by late September. Flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire were suspended, land routes were cut and telecoms were disrupted. The New Humanitarian reported looting of aid warehouses in Mekelle after police withdrew. [18] The ICRC evacuated 161 people from Mekelle to Semera on 28 September. [3]

Nationally, the UN estimated 3.3 million internally displaced in mid-2025, and Ethiopia hosts more than a million refugees. [13] UNHCR data cited by UNICEF puts refugees and asylum seekers at 1,129,183 on 31 August 2026. UNICEF's 2026 appeal needs US$401.5 million and had US$102.9 million by 31 August, a 74 percent gap. It admitted 112,960 children with severe acute malnutrition for treatment in July and August. [30]

FEWS NET's outlook, as of late February, expected Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes in the worst-affected areas and a June to August lean-season peak. It lists East Hararghe lowlands, northern conflict areas and Amhara, Oromia and Afar as concerns, and notes ration cuts in refugee operations. [31] Addis Standard reported in October that Amhara camps face worsening shortages as aid groups scale back. [1]

lenses.local: Addis Standard describes camp residents in Amhara saying aid has largely stopped and appeals to the regional government went unanswered. [1]
lenses.international: AFP and AP say communications cuts make casualty and displacement figures hard to confirm. [7][5]
lenses.scholar: UNICEF and FEWS NET are the main technical sources; neither gives a post-September people-in-need figure, and I did not find the OCHA total. [30][31]

sections.title: Economy: 7.8 percent growth on paper, 11.7 percent inflation, and a debt deal still open
sections.body_md:
The IMF Board completed the fifth review of Ethiopia's Extended Credit Facility on 1 July, allowing an immediate draw of about US$464 million and bringing total disbursements to about US$2.647 billion. About US$200 million was brought forward for higher fuel import costs linked to the Middle East war. [32]

The Fund puts real GDP growth at 7.8 percent for 2025/26, average inflation at 11.7 percent for that year, and reserves at 2.1 months of imports, up from 0.7 months in 2023/24. It projects inflation of 12.3 percent for 2026/27. It welcomed an agreement in principle with Eurobond holders and said bilateral talks with official creditors had signed several agreements. [32]

The Reporter's August opinion piece, summarising an EU Delegation report, says headline inflation rose to 11.7 percent in April from 9.4 percent in March, led by food at 13.5 percent, and that the central bank's roughly 10 percent target looked out of reach. It adds that nominal GDP fell from nearly US$160 billion in 2023 to US$109.1 billion in 2025, which reflects the birr's depreciation. [33]

The war adds risk. Federal fuel and cash restrictions on Tigray were reported in March and July, and Tigray's land routes were cut in September, which raised prices there. [18]

lenses.local: The Reporter's contributor expects the central bank's inflation target to be missed. [33]
lenses.international: Local sourcing is stronger than wire sourcing on the economy; the IMF release is the main outside account. [32]
lenses.scholar: The IMF urges a tight monetary stance, completion of debt restructuring and prudence on new borrowing. [32]

factchecks.claim: Ethiopia's February 2026 letter demanded Eritrea withdraw its troops from the port of Assab, which Ethiopia claims as its own.
factchecks.evidence: AFP obtained the letter, dated 7 February, and Ethiopia's foreign ministry confirmed it. It asks Eritrea to withdraw troops from Tigray and proposes good-faith talks on maritime affairs and sea access through Assab. It does not demand the port's return. Eritrea rejected the accusations on 9 February.

sources.title: Letter accusing Eritrea of troop incursion into Ethiopia taken out of context

factchecks.claim: Eritrean troops are fighting inside Ethiopia alongside the TPLF.
factchecks.by: Ethiopian government and army chief Birhanu Jula; denied by Eritrea's information minister
factchecks.evidence: Ethiopia's foreign minister told the UN Security Council on 8 October of an armed attack, and the army chief says Eritrea leads the rebel offensive. Eritrea denies its troops are in Ethiopia. Critical Threats could not confirm a mobilisation at Sawa or Eritrean fighting near Irob, and a TPLF vice president said the TPLF had no information about Eritrea's plans.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, AFP and Al Jazeera's wire copy file regularly since the September offensive, and Critical Threats, Crisis Group, Chatham House and the Rift Valley Institute produce steady analysis [5][7][8][9]. Coverage is episodic outside big events, and press restrictions leave casualty counts unverified [26][11].

severity.basis: War resumed on 23 September, ACLED counted 253 deaths in Tigray by 21 October, and drone strikes killed at least 25 civilians on 29 to 30 October, with Amhara and Oromia fighting running alongside [18][7][14].
About 761,000 people are displaced in Tigray, 3.3 million nationally as of mid-2025, and UNICEF's appeal was 74 percent unfunded at 31 August [18][13][30].
Editors were detained before the election, opposition parties were kept out, Tigray had no vote, and HRW documents forced recruitment including children of 15 [26][27][34].
The IMF projects 8.2 percent growth for 2026/27 but inflation of 12.3 percent, reserves of 2.1 months of imports and an unfinished debt restructuring [32].
A year ago Pretoria still held on paper; since then the TPLF split, the war resumed, ties with Eritrea were cut and clashes at Rama and Badme continue [12][11][8].

parts.basis: The US special adviser Massad Boulos met Egyptian and Emirati foreign ministers on 13 and 15 November about Horn of Africa security, and the US ambassador joined the Mekelle visit [8].
Ethiopia is a large landlocked economy with a US$2.6 billion IMF programme, a Eurobond restructuring and a Nile dam dispute with Egypt and Sudan [32][15].
Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt are all drawn into the accusations, and Chatham House warns the war may not stay inside Ethiopia [9][8].
Ethiopia hosts 1.13 million refugees and has millions displaced, so instability affects neighbouring humanitarian operations [30][13].
The collapse of an African Union-brokered deal weakens that mediation model, and Chatham House says the AU effort has lost credibility with the TPLF [9].

summary: Ethiopia matters beyond its borders through the Eritrea front, the Sudan war, the Red Sea and Nile disputes with Egypt, and a refugee host role, rather than through trade volumes [8][15][30].
Chatham House expects the conflict to continue for some time and warns of a wider regional war [9].
gi.up: Confirmed large-scale Eritrean or Egyptian involvement, or a federal move on Assab.
gi.down: A negotiated follow-on to Pretoria and a verified Eritrean withdrawal from the border.

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: Tigray Online and Addis Maleda were not retrieved in usable form (Addis Maleda results were non-English pages), and Tigray Broadcast Media was not read.
State-run EBC and Fana were not opened directly; Fana appears only through Critical Threats, and ENA is flagged state_affiliated.
Borkena was read through two pages only (23 and 30 September); its coverage of October and November was not opened.
Casualties in the 2026 Tigray war are unverified; communications cuts and access limits mean no reliable total exists, and ACLED and Frontlines.et figures are second-hand through the UK Home Office.
Fano claims (80 percent of rural Amhara, unified command, foreign drone suppliers) rest on one interview relayed by Addis Standard; the 29 October strike toll rests on residents.
Eritrean troop movements are unconfirmed; Critical Threats could not verify the Sawa mobilisation or Irob fighting.
Ethiopia Insight pieces are viewpoint opinion; the Rift Valley Institute and Chatham House pages name no individual authors.
Reuters and BBC were not opened directly; the 52 Alamata deaths come from BBC via Africanews.
No OCHA people-in-need total was found, and the FEWS NET outlook predates the September war.
Podcast and documentary lengths and the documentary's release year and availability are not stated on the pages seen.
Egypt and GERD detail rests on Al Jazeera and Critical Threats; no Egyptian or Sudanese primary text was read.
